Asymptotic Notation and Growth Comparison

Data Structures and Algorithms · Chapter 2 · Approved English chapter · 18 fully worked problems

1. Scope, prerequisites, and four reviewed university texts

This chapter turns an operation-count function into a defensible statement about its growth. It teaches the precise quantifiers behind upper, lower, tight, and strict bounds; constructive witnesses and disproof; limits and their failure modes; a proved hierarchy of logarithms, powers, exponentials, and factorials; and safe algebra with asymptotic relations. The previous chapter fixed input size and cost model. The next chapters will derive costs from loops and solve recurrences. Those techniques are not silently assumed here. Our default domain is positive integers n tending to infinity, and functions are eventually nonnegative unless a signed variant is expressly given. Elementary algebra, logarithms, induction, and limits are prerequisites; each needed fact is restated when used.

The selected written sources were actually read in their chapter-relevant pages: MIT 6.006 Recitation 1 (PDF pp. 3 and 6), Stanford CS161 Lecture 2 (pp. 6–7), Carnegie Mellon 15-451 Lecture 2 (pp. 10–11), and Kevin Wayne's Princeton algorithm-analysis slides (pp. 3–6). MIT and Stanford supply precise eventual bounds and witness methods; CMU supplies strict notation and oscillation; Princeton supplies algebraic laws, limit proofs, and parameter warnings. They were selected from a bounded pool, documented in the source audit, rather than assumed to be the four globally best courses. The source audit is part of the development record; complete public citations are at the end of this lesson. The exercises below are newly worded; a label saying inspired by identifies a reasoning pattern, not a copied question.

2. The mathematical contract behind a complexity claim

2.1 Which function is being bounded?

Let T(x) be the number of charged primitive operations executed on an instance x. If |x|=n is the specified input-size measure, the worst-case resource function is Tworst(n)=max|x|=nT(x) when the maximum and at least one such input exist. A claim such as Tworst ∈ O(n2) concerns that function under that model and encoding. It does not say every input takes quadratic time, nor does a bound on one algorithm automatically apply to every algorithm for the problem. For an empty size class use a stated alternative, such as a supremum over inputs of size at most n. For average-case cost, first specify an input distribution. For randomized algorithms, specify whether the claim bounds worst-case time over random choices, expectation, or a high-probability event.

Asymptotics ignore a fixed initial segment of sizes. They do not declare a small-input run free or a large constant irrelevant in practice. Consider two hypothetical implementations with costs A(n)=1000n and B(n)=n2. Their symbolic growth classes are Θ(n) and Θ(n2), but B(n)<A(n) for 1<n<1000. The crossover occurs at n=1000. It is a modelling example, not a measured benchmark.

2.2 Function classes are sets

For an eventually nonnegative comparison function g, O(g) is a set of functions. Writing f∈O(g) is formally precise. The conventional notation f=O(g) is read as membership, not ordinary equality; it cannot be algebraically reversed to infer equality of functions. Throughout, choose c,c1,c2>0 and an integer threshold n0 independent of n. A constant may depend on fixed parameters such as a prescribed exponent, but not on the input size it is supposed to bound.

f ∈ O(g) ⇔ ∃c>0, n0 : ∀n≥n0, 0≤f(n)≤c g(n).
f ∈ Ω(g) ⇔ ∃c>0, n0 : ∀n≥n0, 0≤c g(n)≤f(n).
f ∈ Θ(g) ⇔ ∃c1,c2>0,n0 : ∀n≥n0, 0≤c1g(n)≤f(n)≤c2g(n).

The order of quantifiers matters: one pair of constants must work for every sufficiently large input size. “For infinitely many n” is insufficient. For example, f(n)=n2 at odd sizes and f(n)=1 at even sizes satisfies f(n)≥n for infinitely many odd sizes, yet f∉Ω(n) because at arbitrarily large even sizes 1<cn for every fixed c>0. Exchanging f and g gives f∈Ω(g) ⇔ g∈O(f) when the nonnegativity assumptions hold. Tightness means both directions: Θ(g)=O(g)∩Ω(g).

2.3 Strict relations and asymptotic equivalence

In this subsection assume the comparison function g(n)>0 for every sufficiently large n. The little-oh relation is stronger than big-oh:

f ∈ o(g) ⇔ ∀ε>0, ∃nε : ∀n≥nε, 0≤f(n)<εg(n).
f ∈ ω(g) ⇔ ∀M>0, ∃nM : ∀n≥nM, f(n)>Mg(n)≥0.

The strict inequality can be replaced by a non-strict one after changing ε or M; the quantifier over every positive constant is decisive. If g(n)>0 eventually, then f∈o(g) exactly when f(n)/g(n)→0, and f∈ω(g) exactly when the ratio tends to positive infinity. Also f∈ω(g) ⇔ g∈o(f) when both ratios are eventually defined and positive. Neither o(g) nor ω(g) includes a function in Θ(g).

Asymptotic equivalence uses a stronger symbol: f∼g means f(n)/g(n)→1, with g(n)≠0 eventually. Equivalently, |f−g|/g→0 for eventually positive g, or f=g+h with |h|∈o(g). The residual h may be negative: for example, f(n)=n−1 and g(n)=n satisfy f∼g although their difference is −1. This absolute-value formulation respects our nonnegative little-oh convention. Thus f∼g ⇒ f∈Θ(g); the converse is false: 2n∈Θ(n) while 2n∼n is false. “Not in Θ(g)” is not the same as o(g) or ω(g); oscillating or incomparable functions need neither strict relation.

For signed mathematical expressions, some texts define f∈O(g) through |f(n)|≤c|g(n)|. This is useful for error terms but is not the same convention as nonnegative runtime bounds. If a polynomial has a negative leading coefficient, it is eventually negative and cannot itself model elapsed time; first determine whether the intended object is an algebraic error or a nonnegative resource. We use the absolute-value convention only when explicitly stated.

3. Prove or refute a proposed bound

3.1 Construct a witness rather than relying on a slogan

To establish f∈O(g), exhibit constants c,n0 and verify the inequality for every n≥n0. For f(n)=3n2+17n+100 and n≥1, n≤n2 and 1≤n2, so f(n)≤120n2. The lower bound is f(n)≥3n2. Consequently f∈Θ(n2) with c1=3,c2=120,n0=1. These constants are valid, not necessarily optimal. A larger threshold can yield much smaller constants.

For an eventual upper bound, finite exceptions are harmless. For example, n2−100n is negative for some positive sizes, so the runtime convention does not apply there; for n≥101 it is nonnegative and at most n2. A lower bound also needs a threshold: if n≥200, then n2−100n≥n2/2. This yields an eventual Θ claim for the eventually nonnegative function, not a claim about a runtime that is negative on small inputs.

3.2 Negating the quantifiers is the cleanest disproof

To refute f∈O(g) with positive g, show that for every proposed c>0 and n0, some n≥n0 has f(n)>cg(n). For f(n)=n2 and g(n)=n, choose an integer n>max(c,n0). Then n2>cn. A graph of the first few values cannot replace this argument: asymptotic bounds concern an unbounded tail.

Likewise, to refute f∈Ω(g), for every proposed c,n0 find a sufficiently large n with f(n)<cg(n). To refute a Θ claim it is enough to refute either its O or its Ω half. A single exceptional input does not refute an eventual claim; infinitely many unbounded counterexamples can.

3.3 The ratio method and its exact limitations

When g(n)>0 eventually, inspect r(n)=f(n)/g(n). If r(n)→0, then f∈o(g). If r(n)→L for finite L>0, choose ε=L/2 in the limit definition to obtain L/2≤r(n)≤3L/2 eventually; hence f∈Θ(g). If r(n)→∞, then f∈ω(g). If the limit does not exist, return to eventual upper and lower envelopes. A limit is a sufficient classification shortcut, not a necessary condition for Θ.

For example, f(n)=n(2+sin n) has 1≤f(n)/n≤3 for every positive integer, so f∈Θ(n). The ratio has no limit: the integer sequence sin n does not converge. One can avoid needing that nonconvergence fact by using the explicitly alternating f(n)=n for even n and f(n)=3n for odd n; the ratio alternates exactly between 1 and 3, while the Θ witnesses remain 1,3,1. Conversely, a ratio whose liminf is zero and limsup infinite can defeat both O and Ω, as Problem 9 demonstrates.

3.4 Leading terms, cancellations, and discrete transformations

For a nonzero real polynomial p(n)=adnd+⋯+a0 with positive leading coefficient ad, divide by nd: the ratio tends to ad>0, so p∈Θ(nd). If leading terms cancel, simplify the whole expression before reading a degree: (n2+n)−(n2−5n)=6n, not Θ(n2). Do not apply the “largest term wins” rule to a difference of nonnegative terms without controlling cancellation.

For n≥2, n/2≤⌊n/2⌋≤n/2 is false for odd n; a correct robust pair is n/4≤⌊n/2⌋≤n/2. Thus ⌊n/2⌋∈Θ(n). More sharply, ⌊n/2⌋=(n/2)+O(1) using the signed-error convention. Shifts by a fixed constant usually preserve polynomial and logarithmic Θ classes, but not asymptotic equivalence for every family: 2n+1=2·2n is Θ-equivalent to 2n, while their ratio is 2, not 1.

4. Growth classes, with proofs and conditions

4.1 Logarithms and changes of base

For fixed bases a,b>1, the change-of-base identity is logan=(logbn)/(logba). The denominator is a positive constant, hence logan∈Θ(logbn). This does not license discarding a logarithm whose base depends on n: lognn=1 for n>1, whereas log2n grows without bound. Also distinguish log(nk)=k log n from (log n)k, which is generally a different class. We write ln for the natural logarithm and use base 2 when a numerical binary size is intended.

For fixed k>0 and ε>0, (ln n)k∈o(nε). Put t=ln n, so the ratio becomes tke−εt. Choose an integer m>k. The exponential series gives eεt≥(εt)m/m! for t>0. Therefore

0 ≤ tk/eεt ≤ (m!/εm)tk−m → 0.

This proof covers every fixed real k>0, since m can be a larger integer. It also implies log log n∈o(log n) by applying the same fact to t=log n and a positive fractional exponent. The statement is about a fixed k; if k=k(n) increases with input size, redo the analysis.

4.2 Powers and exponentials

For real constants a<b and positive n, na/nb=na−b→0. For fixed bases 1<A<B, An/Bn=(A/B)n→0. More generally, for fixed real a and B>1, na∈o(Bn). If a>0, write Bn=en ln B and reuse the exponential-versus-power argument with t=n; for a≤0 it is immediate from na≤1 for n≥1.

A fixed multiplicative factor outside an exponential disappears inside Θ: 7·2n∈Θ(2n). A change in its exponent's coefficient generally does not: 22n=4n∉Θ(2n), since the ratio is 2n→∞. A fixed shift in the exponent does preserve Θ: Bn+c=BcBn, with Bc a constant. Parentheses matter: 2n2, (2n)2=22n, and 2n2 have different growth rates.

4.3 Factorials and variable exponents

For n≥2, n!=1·2·⋯·n≤nn. At least the last ⌈n/2⌉ factors are at least n/2, giving n!≥(n/2)⌈n/2⌉. Taking logarithms yields an upper bound ln(n!)≤n ln n and a lower bound ln(n!)≥⌈n/2⌉ln(n/2). For n≥4, ln(n/2)≥(ln n)/2, so ln(n!)≥(n/4)ln n. Hence ln(n!)∈Θ(n ln n). This elementary sandwich establishes the class without invoking Stirling's sharper formula.

For any fixed B>1, compare ln(n!/Bn)=ln(n!)−n ln B. The lower bound above tends to infinity, so Bn∈o(n!). Meanwhile n!/nn→0: the first ⌊n/2⌋ factors of n!/nn=∏j=1n(j/n) are at most 1/2, while the rest are at most 1, so the product is at most 2−⌊n/2⌋. Consequently, for fixed positive ε,k and fixed B>1, a useful chain is

1 ≪ log log n ≪ (log n)k ≪ nε ≪ Bn ≪ n! ≪ nn.

Here f≪g abbreviates f∈o(g), and the first relation assumes the logarithms are defined and grow. The chain is illustrative, not a total ordering of every displayed family for every choice of parameters: placing (log n)k after log log n requires fixed k>0; the relative positions of different polynomial powers or different exponential bases need their own comparison. A more granular and unambiguous example is shown below. Each symbol means that the preceding function is little-oh of the following one.

log log n ≪ log n ≪ n1/3 ≪ n ≪ n log n ≪ n2 ≪ 2n ≪ n! ≪ nn

For a nonconstant exponent, taking logarithms is often the safest method: nlog2 n=2(log2 n)2. Its logarithm grows like (ln n)2, faster than the logarithm of every fixed power nc but slower than the logarithm of 2n. Thus for every fixed c>0, nc∈o(nlog2 n) and nlog2 n∈o(2n). The notation 2Θ(n) denotes a family of exponential-order expressions, not an ordinary algebraic value whose Θ can be canceled from an exponent.

5. Algebraic rules and the traps in applying them

5.1 Sum, maximum, product, and transitivity

Suppose f1∈O(g1) and f2∈O(g2), with every function eventually nonnegative. Beyond the larger of the two thresholds, f1+f2≤c1g1+c2g2≤(c1+c2)max(g1,g2). Thus f1+f2∈O(max(g1,g2)). If both summands are nonnegative, max(f1,f2)≤f1+f2≤2max(f1,f2); their sum and maximum are Θ-equivalent. This is the valid “largest term wins” principle for positive costs. Cancellation in a difference is outside its hypotheses.

Multiplication follows from multiplying two nonnegative witness inequalities: f1f2≤c1c2g1g2, so the product is an O bound. If both original relations are Θ, multiply their lower and upper witnesses to get a Θ product. Transitivity also uses shared eventual thresholds: if f≤c1g eventually and g≤c2h eventually, then f≤c1c2h beyond their maximum threshold. Reflexivity f∈Θ(f) holds for an eventually nonnegative f, including the zero function. For fixed c>0, cf∈Θ(f).

These rules do not prove a lower bound for a sum from an upper bound on one summand. They also do not allow subtraction: n2+n and n2−n are each Θ of n2, but their difference is 2n. If f,g>0 eventually and f∈Θ(g), dividing the two-sided witnesses gives 1/f∈Θ(1/g). A mere f∈O(g) gives a reciprocal lower bound when f>0, not necessarily reciprocal Θ; for example 1∈O(n) but 1∉Θ(1/n) after reciprocation.

5.2 Composition, logarithms of costs, and nonmonotone functions

If f∈O(g) and h maps large inputs to values tending to infinity, then f(h(n))∈O(g(h(n))), assuming h(n) lies in the domain. The condition matters: if h(n)=1 forever, the eventual part of the original bound tells us nothing about the composed values. If f∈Θ(g), the same condition preserves Θ. An arbitrary outer function cannot be applied to both sides of an O relation: from f≤cg one cannot conclude 2f∈O(2g). Take f=2n, g=n; f∈Θ(g), but 22n∉O(2n). Even a monotone outer operation may amplify a constant factor into a changing one.

If positive f∈Θ(g) and both grow beyond 1, logarithms have an additive constant difference, since ln c1+ln g≤ln f≤ln c2+ln g. If ln g→∞, then ln f∼ln g. If g tends to 1, logarithmic comparison can break: f=2, g=1 are Θ-equivalent, yet ln f is positive and ln g=0. State positivity and growth before taking logarithms of a complexity bound.

5.3 Two or more independent size parameters

For functions of n,m, define a claim relative to an admissible domain D⊆ℕ². One precise joint-tail convention says f∈OD(g) if constants c,N,M>0 exist such that 0≤f(n,m)≤cg(n,m) for every (n,m)∈D with both n≥N and m≥M. An alternative one-size measure could use n+m→∞; it is a different convention and can include paths with one parameter fixed. Name the convention before comparing multivariate functions. If a graph has n vertices and m edges, restrictions such as 0≤m≤n(n−1)/2 for a simple undirected graph belong in D. It is invalid to replace m by n without an assumption that relates them.

On unconstrained positive integer pairs, n+m∉O(n): choose m=n2, making the ratio 1+n unbounded. On the restricted domain m≤3n, n+m≤4n, so n+m∈Θ(n) because it is also at least n. A one-variable hierarchy is not a substitute for checking every allowed growth path.

Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Decide the relation before comparing growth

For eventually positive g, f∈O(g) means one constant upper bound on f/g beyond some threshold. f∈Ω(g) means an eventual positive lower bound; Θ requires both. Little-oh requires f/g→0, a strictly stronger conclusion than boundedness. A positive finite ratio limit proves Θ, but the absence of a limit does not refute Θ: a ratio oscillating between 1 and 3 is still bounded above and below.

Transform exponents and logarithms exactly

For fixed positive bases with logarithms defined, alogbn=nlogba. This is an exact identity obtained by taking natural logarithms. In contrast, alogb2n has exponent proportional to (lnn)2 and grows faster than every fixed polynomial. Constants inside an exponent are not multiplicative constants outside it: 22n/2n=2n is unbounded.

For fixed integer r, (nr)=Θ(nr) because the numerator is a product of r linear factors and r! is constant. If r grows with n, this reasoning fails. In particular, central binomial coefficients are exponential up to a polynomial factor; the fixed-index theorem must not be silently generalized.

Cancellation and several variables need their own analysis

Knowing f,g∈Θ(n2) does not determine f-g: cancellation can leave zero, a linear term or an oscillatory residual. For two independent parameters, a proposed O(n) bound on n+m fails on the path m=n2. Conversely, n+m∈Θ(max(n,m)) follows from the two inequalities max(n,m)≤n+m≤2max(n,m). Choose parameter paths to refute a uniform claim.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

Each problem states what must be decided and why each step is valid. “Inspired by” identifies a source's technique; the statement and solution are original. These are instructional worked problems, not a request that the student answer a test before completing the first reading.

Tutorial 1 — Exhibit both witnesses for a polynomial

Task. Establish a tight bound for F(n)=7n3−5n2+12n+9, with explicit constants.

Solution. For n≥1, upper-bound each positive term by its cubic counterpart and discard the negative term: F(n)≤(7+12+9)n3=28n3. For the lower bound, 7n3−5n2=n2(7n−5)≥2n3 because 7n−5≥2n for n≥1. The remaining terms are nonnegative. Thus 2n3≤F(n)≤28n3 for every n≥1. The witnesses c1=2,c2=28,n0=1 prove F∈Θ(n3). A leading-term limit also works, but this construction directly verifies the definition. Technique inspired by Stanford CS161's polynomial witnesses.

Tutorial 2 — Refute an overoptimistic upper bound

Task. Decide whether n3+4n∈O(n2 log2n).

Solution. The ratio is (n3+4n)/(n2log2n)=n/log2n+4/(n log2n) for n>1. The first term tends to infinity because log2n∈o(n), proved in §4.1; the second is nonnegative. Hence no fixed upper constant can work, so the membership is false. Directly, for any c choose n so large that n/log2n>c, then n3+4n>cn2log2n. This refutes the eventual universal quantifier, not merely a finite sample.

Tutorial 3 — Little-oh versus big-oh

Task. Classify F(n)=n(log2n)3 relative to G(n)=n5/4, and explain why a finite positive ratio would change the answer.

Solution. Cancel the positive n: F/G=(log2n)3/n1/4→0 by the logarithm-versus-power proof, with fixed k=3,ε=1/4. Therefore F∈o(G), hence also F∈O(G), but F∉Ω(G). If instead the ratio tended to a fixed positive number, the lower and upper witness constants would both exist and the correct relation would be Θ rather than little-oh.

Tutorial 4 — Fix a broken logarithm-base shortcut

Task. Compare F(n)=lognn2 with G(n)=log2n on n≥2.

Solution. By definition lognn2=2. Thus F/G=2/log2n→0, proving F∈o(G). The usual assertion that logarithm bases differ only by a constant applies only when those bases are fixed independently of n. Here the base is the variable input size. The exact value 2 also makes clear that F∈Θ(1).

Tutorial 5 — Exponent position changes everything

Task. Order 2n3, (2n)3, and 2n3 by strict asymptotic growth.

Solution. The middle expression is 23n=8n. A polynomial is little-oh of a fixed-base exponential, so 2n3∈o(8n). For the remaining pair, the ratio 8n/2n3=23n−n3→0 because n3−3n→∞. Thus 2n3 ≪ (2n)3 ≪ 2n3. Parentheses are essential: the first expression has a constant coefficient, the second has a linear exponent, and the third has a cubic exponent. Reasoning type informed by MIT 6.006's exponential-comparison exercises.

Tutorial 6 — A binomial coefficient with a fixed lower index

Task. For a fixed integer r≥1, find a tight class of C(n,r) as n→∞.

Solution. The exact product is C(n,r)=n(n−1)⋯(n−r+1)/r!. Since r is fixed, r! is a constant. Divide by nr: the ratio is (1/r!)∏j=0r−1(1−j/n)→1/r!>0, because the finite product has r factors, each tending to 1. Therefore C(n,r)∈Θ(nr), and more sharply C(n,r)∼nr/r!. If r=r(n) grows, this finite-fixed-product proof no longer applies. Reasoning type informed by MIT 6.006's fixed-index binomial comparison.

Tutorial 7 — Cancellation defeats a naive dominant-term rule

Task. Simplify and classify F(n)=(n3+4n2+1)−(n3−2n2+n).

Solution. Expand the subtraction before applying any growth rule: F(n)=6n2−n+1. The leading surviving coefficient is positive, so dividing by n2 gives 6−1/n+1/n2→6. Thus F∈Θ(n2), and indeed F∼6n2. Treating each parenthesis as Θ of n3 and subtracting Θ classes would lose the cancellation and produce an unjustified answer.

Tutorial 8 — A nonexistent limit with a valid tight bound

Task. Let F(n)=4n for even n and F(n)=9n for odd n. Classify it relative to n and decide whether it is asymptotically equivalent to 6n.

Solution. Every positive n satisfies 4n≤F(n)≤9n, so F∈Θ(n). The ratio F(n)/(6n) alternates between 2/3 and 3/2, so it does not tend to 1; F∼6n is false. Lack of a ratio limit did not defeat Θ because two global envelopes hold. Technique informed by CMU's oscillation example and Princeton's limit counterexample.

Tutorial 9 — Functions that are genuinely incomparable

Task. Define F(n)=n for even n and F(n)=n3 for odd n. Compare F with G(n)=n2.

Solution. On even sizes F/G=1/n→0, so no positive constant can lower-bound the ratio on all sufficiently large sizes; F∉Ω(G). On odd sizes F/G=n→∞, so no fixed constant can upper-bound it on all sufficiently large sizes; F∉O(G). Therefore F∉Θ(G) and neither function is uniformly no faster or no slower under these one-sided relations. This is different from Problem 8, where the oscillation stayed within fixed factors.

Tutorial 10 — Take factorial logarithms without overclaiming

Task. Classify H(n)=log2((3n)!) relative to n log2n, for integer n≥1.

Solution. Section 4.3 proved ln(k!)∈Θ(k ln k). Apply it with k=3n: ln((3n)!)∈Θ(3n ln(3n)). Since ln(3n)=ln n+ln3∈Θ(ln n) for n≥2, this is Θ of n ln n. Dividing by fixed ln2 changes only the constant, so H∈Θ(n log2n). This does not imply (3n)!∈Θ(n!); factorials themselves are much more sensitive to the argument.

Tutorial 11 — Show a factorial ratio is unbounded

Task. Decide whether (2n)!∈O(n!) and whether their logarithms have the same Θ class.

Solution. The ratio is (2n)!/n!=∏j=n+12nj≥(n+1)n→∞, so (2n)!∉O(n!) and hence cannot be Θ of n!. Yet ln((2n)!)∈Θ(2n ln(2n))=Θ(n ln n) and ln(n!)∈Θ(n ln n), so the two logarithms are Θ-equivalent. A logarithm compresses a multiplicative gap into an additive one; equal logarithmic Θ classes do not imply equal original Θ classes. Reasoning type informed by MIT 6.006's factorial comparison.

Tutorial 12 — Compare a variable exponent to both neighboring classes

Task. For each fixed c>0, compare nc, nlog2n, and 2n.

Solution. Take base-two logarithms of ratios, which preserves their order because log2 is strictly increasing. For the first ratio, log2(nlog2n/nc)=(log2n)2−c log2n→∞; hence nc∈o(nlog2n). For the second, log2(2n/nlog2n)=n−(log2n)2→∞ by the logarithm-versus-power theorem. Thus nlog2n∈o(2n). The middle expression is superpolynomial for every fixed degree but subexponential relative to base 2 in this precise comparison.

Tutorial 13 — Floors, ceilings, and fixed shifts

Task. Determine the class of F(n)=⌈n/3⌉+⌊√n⌋, and decide whether F∼n/3.

Solution. The elementary floor/ceiling inequalities give n/3≤⌈n/3⌉<n/3+1 and √n−1<⌊√n⌋≤√n. Therefore n/3≤F(n)<n/3+1+√n for positive integers. Dividing by n/3 gives 1≤F(n)/(n/3)<1+3/n+3/√n→1. The squeeze theorem proves the sharper statement F∼n/3, which implies F∈Θ(n). The square-root and rounding errors are genuinely lower order; no exact equality was assumed.

Tutorial 14 — A two-parameter path invalidates a one-parameter guess

Task. On unconstrained positive integer pairs, decide whether F(n,m)=n2+m belongs to O(n2). Re-evaluate on D={(n,m):1≤m≤n2}.

Solution. On the unconstrained domain choose the allowed path m=n3. Then F/n2=1+n→∞, refuting a universal fixed constant. On D, n2≤F≤2n2, so F∈ΘD(n2) with witnesses 1,2. The answer changes because the domain changes; a bound on one path cannot establish a multivariate bound over all paths. Reasoning type informed by Princeton's multiple-parameter slides.

Tutorial 15 — Exposing an invalid subtraction of Θ classes

Task. Decide whether the information A∈Θ(n2) and B∈Θ(n2) determines the class of A−B.

Solution. It does not. Three examples, all with nonnegative A,B, show why. If A=n2 and B=n2, their difference is identically zero. If A=n2+n and B=n2, the difference is n∈Θ(n). If A=2n2 and B=n2, the difference is n2∈Θ(n2). All three satisfy the same two premises. One must analyze the actual expressions or establish additional information, such as their leading coefficients or a bound on the difference.

Tutorial 16 — An algorithm's upper bound and a problem's lower bound

Task. A problem has a proved worst-case lower bound Ω(n log n) for every algorithm in a stated comparison model. Algorithm A has a proved worst-case upper bound O(n log n) in the same model. What follows? What if its upper bound were only O(n2)?

Solution. The universal problem lower bound applies to A in that model. Combined with its upper bound, TA,worst∈Θ(n log n), and no algorithm in that model can have an asymptotically smaller worst-case order than this lower bound. If the only upper bound on A is O(n2), then we know TA,worst∈Ω(n log n)∩O(n2), but no Θ class follows: n log n, n3/2, and n2 all fit those one-sided constraints. A lower bound on one algorithm alone would not establish a problem lower bound. Reasoning type informed by CMU's asymptotic optimality discussion.

Tutorial 17 — Composition and exponentiation are different moves

Task. Given f(t)=2t and g(t)=t, let h(n)=⌊√n⌋. Compare f∘h with g∘h, then compare 2f(n) with 2g(n).

Solution. Because f(t)=2g(t) for every t, substitution gives f(h(n))=2g(h(n)); hence they are Θ-equivalent. The fact that h(n)→∞ also satisfies the general composition condition. Exponentiating the values is a different operation: 2f(n)/2g(n)=2n→∞. Therefore 2f(n)∉O(2g(n)). A fixed multiplicative difference in exponents is not a fixed multiplicative difference in exponentials.

Tutorial 18 — Tightness, equivalence, and a finite crossover

Task. Compare P(n)=400n+20 and Q(n)=n2+20 both asymptotically and at n=100. Determine whether P∼400n.

Solution. P(n)/n=400+20/n→400, so P∈Θ(n); Q(n)/n2=1+20/n2→1, so Q∈Θ(n2). Thus P/Q→0 and P∈o(Q). At n=100, however, P(100)=40020 while Q(100)=10020; the quadratic expression is smaller there. Their difference is P−Q=400n−n2=n(400−n), so the positive-size crossover is n=400. Finally, P/(400n)=1+1/(20n)→1, so P∼400n. The fixed numbers describe these symbolic functions only; no hardware performance follows without measuring implementations.

Mathematical constructions for uniform growth claims

1. Construct a threshold and quantify what it proves

Consider F(n)=3n2+5n. Its normalized ratio is 3+5/n. To prove an upper bound with a prescribed constant c>3, solve 5/n≤c-3, giving n≥5/(c-3). A convenient integer threshold is max(1,⌈5/(c-3)⌉). At c=3, the inequality fails at every finite positive size. The limit three is the infimum of valid eventual upper constants, not an attained witness.

To prove equivalence to 3n2, normalize by the full proposed equivalent: F/(3n2)=1+5/(3n). For each error ε>0, choose n>5/(3ε). This establishes a ratio tending to one. Equivalence to n2 fails because that ratio tends to three, even though both reference functions have the same tight class. These witness calculations explain the difference among exact arithmetic, one-sided bounds, tightness and equivalence.

A negative result has a different quantifier order. To refute n2∈O(n), defeat every proposed c,N by choosing an integer n>max(c,N). Such a choice makes n2>cn. Finding one bad small input does not accomplish that universal disproof.

2. Classify an oscillating ratio using two envelopes

Assume g(n)>0 eventually and put r(n)=f(n)/g(n)≥0. An eventual finite upper bound on r characterizes O(g); an eventual positive lower bound characterizes Ω(g). Both characterize Θ(g). A unique limit is unnecessary for these envelope tests.

For F(k)=k(2+(-1)k), the ratio to k is one or three, and 1≤r(k)≤3 supplies tight witnesses. For f(n)=n on evens and n2 on odds, the ratio to n is one or n; its upper envelope is unbounded, excluding O(n). Relative to n2, the ratio is 1/n or one; it has no eventual positive lower envelope, excluding Ω(n2).

For a genuinely incomparable pair, use f(n)=n on evens and n3 on odds against g(n)=n2. The even ratios tend to zero and the odd ratios to infinity. This defeats both one-sided bounds, while neither strict ratio limit exists. The normalized samples in the question animations illustrate these different envelope behaviors; the subsequence arguments prove the tail statements.

3. Exponentiate a difference, not a broad growth class

For fixed a>1, the exact quotient au(n)/av(n)=au(n)-v(n) controls every relation. The original exponentials are tightly equivalent exactly when the exponent difference is bounded above and below eventually. If the difference tends to positive infinity, the first exponential is strict larger order; if it tends to negative infinity, it is strict smaller order. A bounded oscillating difference preserves tightness even if the ratio has no limit.

The distinction is visible for u=n2+n and v=n2. Their ratio tends to one, but their difference tends to infinity. Thus their exponentials are not tightly equivalent. Conversely, u=n+(-1)n and v=n have bounded difference, so their base-two exponentials have ratios alternating between one half and two, proving tightness without equivalence.

Logarithms are also conditional. If f,g>0 eventually and f∈Θ(g), then lnf-lng is bounded. If additionally g→∞, dividing that bounded difference by lng proves lnf∼lng. Without that growth premise, take f=2 and g=1: the original functions are tightly equivalent but their logarithms are not. The reverse implication fails for growing functions too, as the preceding quadratic-exponent example shows.

4. Derive harmonic bounds from decreasing rectangles

For 1/x decreasing on positive arguments, its integral over [k,k+1] is at most 1/k. Summing these rectangles gives ln(n+1)≤Hn. On [k-1,k] for k≥2, the integral is at least 1/k. Summing and separating the first term gives Hn≤1+lnn.

These are rigorous lower and upper bounds. On n>1, dividing by lnn yields a ratio trapped between ln(n+1)/lnn and 1+1/lnn, both tending to one. Consequently Hn∼lnn. It is still false that Hn=lnn: the finite rational sum and the logarithm are distinct quantities.

Grouping terms gives another proof of divergence. The block k=2j-1+1,…,2j contains 2j-1 terms, each at least 2-j, so every complete block contributes at least one half. The number of such blocks up to n is logarithmic. This argument explains why infinitely many shrinking positive increments can accumulate an unbounded but sublinear sum.

5. Separate fixed parameters from uniformly varying parameters

A witness constant for a one-variable family can depend on a truly fixed coefficient, exponent or logarithm base. It cannot depend on the input variable. In a two-variable bound, decide whether both variables exceed their own thresholds or whether a single combined size tends to infinity; these are different tail conventions.

For T(m,n)=mlog2n+n with independent m,n≥2, both contributions must remain. Along m=n2, the first dominates; along m=⌊n⌋, the second dominates; both paths grow both variables and remain admissible under the joint-tail convention. Neither single term uniformly replaces the sum. The pointwise maximum does: for nonnegative A,B, max(A,B)≤A+B≤2max(A,B).

If a constraint supplies m=n, the same expression reduces to tight nlogn order. If m≤n/(log2n), it instead has tight linear order in n. Changing the domain can change the answer even when the algebraic function is unchanged. State those restrictions before simplifying a graph, matrix or multivariate running time.

6. Interpret the retained model animations precisely

The threshold animation uses F(n)=3n+7 and candidate upper envelope 4n. Its normalized ratio is 3+7/n. The inequality is equivalent to n≥7, not to every positive input. The saved checkpoints at one, two and four show finite exceptions; eight, sixteen and thirty-two show inputs beyond the threshold. Their success alone is not the proof: solving the inequality supplies the universal tail statement.

The encoding animation compares the numerical parameter 2k with its ordinary binary length k+1. The doubling animation visits 1,2,4,8,16 under the guard x<17, then exits at 32. Together they illustrate a fixed number of logarithmic stages versus the numerical sizes visited. They do not prove an arbitrary program's cost merely from its largest value, and do not represent the authentic square-root recurrence.

The separate recurrence-tree animation uses the explicitly different model T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, with n=8 and T(1)=1. Internal levels contain one, two and four calls with sizes eight, four and two; the final level contains eight unit-cost base calls. Every displayed level therefore contributes eight, giving total cost thirty-two. Its equal-size splitting and linear toll are stated assumptions. It is an introduction to level accounting, not a simulation of either unequal splitting or the square-root recurrence in the authentic questions.

The question-specific oscillation and binary-floor animations below use each question's actual normalized functions. Their axes label the input and ratio explicitly, and their captions distinguish saved finite samples from the general subsequence proofs. Points on a discrete domain are not a continuous interpolation theorem.

This bank combines authentic Iranian entrance-examination questions, newly authored medium/hard analogues, and two retained multistep challenges. The original four-option numbering is retained for authentic questions. Difficulty labels for original problems are qualitative author judgments, not calibrated response statistics.

Authentic examinations · Original analogues · Integrated challenges

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q1 — Unequal recursive splits

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 1. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Fixed positive constants α,β satisfy α+β=1. For T(n)=T(αn)+T(βn)+n with constant small-input base cost, which listed bound is correct?

1.
O(αβn)
2.
O(nlogn)
3.
O(βnαlogn)
4.
O(αn+βlogn)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 2. The hypotheses make both shrink factors fixed numbers strictly between zero and one. This matters: the recurrence describes two unequal children whose sizes sum to their parent's size, rather than two equal children. Let B>0 be a fixed stopping size, δ=min(α,β) and q=max(α,β). First consider exact real-size splits so their tree geometry is visible.

Every node at depth j has size between nδj and nqj. Before nδj reaches B, all nodes at that depth are internal. Their sizes sum to n, because splitting conserves size. Consequently each such full level contributes exactly n units of nonrecursive work. There are Θ(lnn) full levels, with the constant depending on the fixed δ. This supplies the lower bound Ω(nlnn).

Every path terminates once nqj≤B, which requires only O(lnn) levels. At a partly terminated level, the active-node sizes sum to at most n. Therefore all internal tolls total O(nlnn). A nonroot leaf has size greater than δB and at most B, because its parent exceeded B. Leaf sizes sum to n, so there are Θ(n) leaves; their bounded base costs add at most linear work. Both bounds establish T(n)∈Θ(nlnn).

For ordinary integer rounding, the same order follows from the standard bounded-perturbation version of the divide-and-conquer recurrence theorem. Its branching exponent solves αp+βp=1: here p=1, and the toll integral is ∫1nu/u2du=lnn. This application requires fixed shrink factors, a fixed base region and the usual bounded rounding errors; it is not an assertion for arbitrary size-dependent perturbations.

Options 1 and 4 have linear order because α,β are constants and lnn=O(n). They cannot upper-bound the derived cost. Option 3 is also too small: its ratio to nlnn is βnα-1→0. Option 2 is the valid listed upper bound. If α were permitted to approach zero with n, the fixed-depth constants used above would cease to be uniform.

Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q2 — A polylogarithmic toll

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 2. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

What is the order of T(n)=T(2n/3)+log2n, with bounded base cost?

1.
Θ(n)
2.
Θ(log2n)
3.
Θ(log3n)
4.
Θ(nlog2n)

Source correction. The fourth option was rechecked against the original PDF and restored to include the factor n and the squared logarithm.

Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 3. Take logarithms in one fixed base; changing that base multiplies the toll by a fixed positive constant. Put L=lnn and a=ln(3/2)>0. After j exact recursive reductions, the argument is (2/3)jn, so its logarithm is L-ja. With a fixed base threshold, the number of nonbase levels is h=L/a+O(1).

Unrolling the single chain gives

T(n)=O(1)+∑j=0h-1(L-ja)2.

There are O(L) terms, each at most L2, proving O(L3). For a lower bound, consider only 0≤j≤L/(2a), leaving aside a fixed endpoint adjustment. There are Θ(L) such terms, and each has L-ja≥L/2. Their sum is at least a positive fixed multiple of L3. Thus T(n)∈Θ((lnn)3).

A concrete exact subsequence checks the accumulation. For n=(3/2)h and a base at one, the toll sum is a2∑r=1hr2=a2h(h+1)(2h+1)/6. The cubic power comes from summing squared decreasing logarithms, not from multiplying arbitrary complexity symbols.

Option 2 counts only the largest toll, omitting the many other large tolls. Option 4 multiplies a root-sized squared-logarithm toll by a linear number of inputs rather than a logarithmic number of levels: its proposed tight order is Θ(nlog2n), whose ratio to the actual cost grows as n/logn. Option 1 is a loose upper bound for sufficiently large n, but it asserts a tight linear order, which fails because (lnn)3/n→0. In this question the options use Θ, so a loose upper bound does not make another option correct. Rounding the argument must still guarantee eventual reduction into the fixed base region.

Question 3. MSc CE 1405, Q58 — A square-root recurrence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 13 · question 58. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Which listed bound describes T(n)=2T(⌊n⌋)+logn with bounded base cost?

1.
O(lognloglogn)
2.
O(nloglogn)
3.
O(loglogn)
4.
O(logn)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 1 under the smallest-listed-upper-bound convention. The tight order is Θ(lnnlnlnn). The original options use O, so option 2 is a valid looser upper bound as well. Preserve that wording ambiguity when using this authentic question; the derivation identifies the tight order without treating two true upper bounds as logically exclusive.

Let m=log2n. Ignoring rounding momentarily, taking a square root halves m, so S(m)=T(2m) satisfies S(m)=2S(m/2)+m. At depth j, there are 2j nodes, each with toll m/2j. Total toll is exactly m per nonbase level. There are Θ(logm) levels, and the leaves contribute O(m) bounded base work. Hence S(m)∈Θ(mlogm).

The floor does not invalidate this reasoning, but it requires control. Use a constant base region containing one and two. For x≥4, x/2≤⌊x⌋≤x. Taking base-two logarithms gives

m/2-1≤log2⌊x⌋≤m/2.

Repeated reduction bounds a level- j logarithmic argument between m/2j-2 and m/2j. Therefore a level's toll is at most m, and, while 2j≤m/4, at least m-2j+1≥m/2. There are Θ(logm) significant levels and only O(m) leaves, giving matching upper and lower bounds despite rounding. Small endpoint levels alter constants only. Stopping solely below one would fail to terminate at one because its square root remains one.

Substitution returns mlogm=Θ(lognloglogn). Option 3 omits the logn factor; option 4 omits the loglogn factor. Option 2 grows much faster, so it is true as an upper bound but not tight. On n=22h, all square roots are exact until the base, providing the independent check S(2h)/2h=S(1)+h under a unit base-two logarithmic toll.

Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q71 — A multiplicative one-step recurrence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 71. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

For T(n)=2nT(n-1) and T(0)=1, which listed order is correct?

1.
Θ(n2n)
2.
Θ(2nlogn)
3.
Θ(2n2)
4.
Θ((2)n2+n)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 4. This recurrence multiplies the previous value by a changing factor. Its expansion is a product, unlike an additive-toll recurrence:

T(n)=2n2n-1…21T(0)=21+2+…+n=2n(n+1)/2.

The base value T(0)=1 is essential for this exact identity. Taking a base-two logarithm gives the simple additive relation log2T(n)-log2T(n-1)=n, with zero initial logarithm.

n Multiplying factor Exact T(n) log2T(n)
0 Base 1 0
1 2 2 1
2 4 8 3
3 8 64 6
4 16 1024 10

The fourth expression is exactly (2)n2+n=2(n2+n)/2. For option 3, dividing its candidate by the exact result gives 2(n2-n)/2→∞, so it is not a tight class. Option 2 has logarithm n+log2logn, which is negligible beside the quadratic exact logarithm. Option 1 has logarithm 2nlog2n; since (logn)/n→0, it too is much smaller than the true value.

The tempting replacement 2n(n+1)/2∈Θ(2n2) is false. The exponent itself has quadratic order, but exponentiation amplifies a constant-factor difference in that exponent into an unbounded ratio. Writing T=2Θ(n2) is a valid broad family description; it does not select the tighter fourth expression automatically.

Question 5. Two true upper bounds but one tight class

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q58; Phd_CE_1405_Q1. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let f(n)=nlogn+n3/4. Which conjunction is correct?

1.

f∈Θ(n) and f∈O(nlogn)

2.

f∈Θ(nlogn) and f∈O(n2)

3.

f∈o(nlogn) and f∈O(n2)

4.

f∈Θ(n2) and f∈O(nlogn)

Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 2. Work on n≥2, where the fixed-base logarithm is positive. Normalize by the proposed leading term:

nlogn+n3/4nlogn=1+1n1/4logn→1.

For sufficiently large n, the ratio lies, for example, between one and two. These are actual lower and upper constant witnesses, proving f∈Θ(nlogn). Also logn=O(n) and n3/4≤n2, so f∈O(n2). That second statement is deliberately loose.

Option 1 fails because f/n=logn+n-1/4→∞, refuting the upper half of Θ(n). Option 3 fails because the first displayed ratio tends to one rather than zero. Option 4 fails because f/n2=(logn)/n+n-5/4→0, refuting Ω(n2). Thus a true larger upper bound and a correct smaller tight class can coexist without contradiction.

The lower-order summand remains positive at every finite n; discarding it means classifying growth, not claiming equality. If a question asked the exact value or a finite crossover, retain it. If the exponent 3/4 were replaced by an input-dependent exponent, its comparison would require a fresh argument.

Question 6. A factor inside an exponential cannot be suppressed

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q71. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Which statement is correct for f(n)=2n2+n and g(n)=2n2?

1.
f∈Θ(g)
2.
f∈o(g)
3.
g∈o(f)
4.
f/g=n
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 3. Divide the exponentials before comparing them:

f(n)g(n)=2n2+n2n2=2n,g(n)f(n)=2-n→0.

The latter ratio proves g∈o(f) directly. For every ε>0, choose an integer threshold exceeding log2(1/ε); all later ratios are below ε. Conversely, for every proposed upper constant c, an integer n>log2c makes f(n)>cg(n). Therefore f∉O(g) and cannot be in Θ(g).

Option 2 reverses the strict relation. Option 4 replaces an exponential quotient by the exponent difference; subtraction produces n inside the power of two, not as the final ratio. At n=3, the ratio is eight, already illustrating that distinction.

Both logarithms have quadratic order: log2f=n2+n and log2g=n2. They are even asymptotically equivalent, yet the original functions are not tightly equivalent. The correct exact criterion for fixed base a>1 is that au(n)/av(n)=au(n)-v(n) stay bounded above and below by fixed positive constants. This is equivalent to a bounded exponent difference, not merely u∈Θ(v).

Question 7. Oscillation defeats a tight bound

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q2; MS_CE_1405_Q58. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

f(n)=n for even n and n2 for odd n. Which classification is correct?

1.
f∈Θ(n)
2.
f∈Θ(n2)
3.

f∈O(n2)∩Ω(n) but neither listed tight class

4.
f∉O(n2)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 3. For every positive integer, n≤f(n)≤n2, giving the declared Ω(n) and O(n2) bounds with constant one and threshold one. Tightness requires a second inequality on all sufficiently large integers.

Subsequence f(n)/n f(n)/n2 Consequence
Even n=2k 1 1/(2k) No positive eventual quadratic lower constant
Odd n=2k+1 2k+1 1 No finite eventual linear upper constant

To refute O(n), let any c>0 and threshold N be proposed. Choose an odd integer n>max(c,N). Then f(n)=n2>cn. To refute Ω(n2), choose an even n>max(1/c,N). Then f(n)=n<cn2. These constructions defeat arbitrary proposed witnesses, rather than a few numerical samples.

Option 1 therefore fails its upper half; option 2 fails its lower half; option 4 contradicts the explicit valid quadratic upper bound. The two subsequences are both unbounded, so neither can be omitted as a finite exception. Also do not infer f∈o(n2): its normalized ratio remains one on odd sizes. An absent tight class does not automatically produce a strict growth relation.

The complete derivation and assumptions are written above.

Question 8. Cancellation before classifying a function

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q58; Phd_CE_1405_Q2. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For positive integers n, simplify the growth of f(n)=n2+n-n.

1.
Θ(n)
2.
Θ(n)
3.
Θ(1)
4.
Θ(1/n)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 3. Directly assigning linear order to each large term would ignore their subtraction. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate:

n2+n-n=(n2+n)-n2n2+n+n=11+1/n+1.

For n≥1, 1≤1+1/n≤2, so

12+1≤f(n)<12.

These positive constants establish a tight constant order immediately. The denominator tends to two, giving the sharper limit f(n)→1/2; it is not exactly one half for any finite positive n.

Option 1 predicts unbounded linear growth, option 2 unbounded square-root growth, and option 4 decay to zero. Each contradicts the explicit positive constant sandwich. For another check, at n=1 the value is 2-1, and rationalizing yields the same lower-end value 1/(2+1).

More generally, for fixed a>0, n2+an-n→a/2 by the same calculation. Changing the added term to one instead of n gives n2+1-n=1/(n2+1+n)∈Θ(1/n). This pair explains precisely when option 4 would become appropriate: the numerator left after cancellation has changed.

Question 9. Logarithmic change of variable

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q58; Phd_CS_1404_Q71. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Which order belongs to n1/log2n for n>1?

1.
Θ(n)
2.
Θ(logn)
3.
Θ(1)
4.
Θ(1/logn)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 3. The exponent is not a fixed polynomial degree. For n>1, let t=log2n>0. Then n=2t and

n1/log2n=(2t)1/t=2.

This is an exact identity, so the function has tight constant order. Equivalently, its natural logarithm is (lnn)/(log2n)=ln2, confirming the same value without numerical approximation.

Options 1 and 2 describe functions growing without bound; option 4 describes a function tending to zero. None can be tightly equivalent to the constant two. At n=2,4,16, the powers are respectively 21, 41/2 and 161/4, all two. These examples check the grouping, while the algebra proves the identity for the entire domain.

At n=1, the exponent contains division by zero; the original domain correctly excludes it. For any fixed logarithm base b>1, the corresponding expression is exactly b. If the base varies with n, so does that result: a variable-base expression cannot be classified using fixed-base shorthand. A useful related identity is nc/logbn=bc for fixed c and admissible n.

Question 10. Independent parameters forbid a one-variable collapse

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q1; MS_CS_1405_Q113. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For integers m,n≥2, T(m,n)=mlogn+n. Which uniform bound is tight?

1.
Θ(mlogn+n)
2.
Θ(nlogn)
3.
Θ(mn)
4.
Θ(mlogn)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 1. The declared expression retains two independent nonnegative contributions. Under a uniform bound on admissible pairs, constants cannot depend on either growing input parameter. The original lesson uses a joint-tail convention: both m and n exceed independently chosen fixed thresholds. The following counterexamples grow both parameters, so they also work under that stricter convention.

For option 2, take m=n2. Then

T(m,n)nlogn=n+1logn→∞.

Thus no uniform upper constant for that class exists. For option 4, use m=⌊n⌋. Its ratio is T/(mlogn)=1+n/(mlogn), which diverges because n/logn→∞. The omitted additive n term can dominate even though both parameters tend to infinity.

Option 3 is a valid broad upper bound: for base-two logarithms and m,n≥2, mlog2n+n≤mn+mn/2. But along m=n, the ratio to mn is (logn+1)/n→0, refuting the matching lower bound and hence the proposed Θ(mn) class. Other fixed bases merely change constants.

Option 1 is tight by equality, with lower and upper witness one. It can equivalently be written Θ(max(mlogn,n)), since the sum of two nonnegative terms lies between their maximum and twice that maximum. A restriction such as m=n would allow simplification to Θ(nlogn), but that relationship is absent from this question.

Question 11. The floor in an exponent

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q2; MS_CE_1405_Q58. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Compare f(n)=2⌊log2n⌋ to n. Which bounds hold for all positive n?

1.
n/2<f(n)≤n
2.
n≤f(n)<2n
3.
f(n)=n
4.
f(n)≤log2n
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 1. Define k=⌊log2n⌋. The defining floor interval gives k≤log2n<k+1. Exponentiating the entire interval, using monotonicity, yields 2k≤n<2k+1. Rearranging gives

n/2<2k=f(n)≤n.

These are exact bounds for every positive integer, including n=1. In particular, f∈Θ(n) with witnesses one half and one. Equality at the upper endpoint holds precisely when n is a power of two.

At n=3, f=2, refuting option 2's reversed lower bound and option 3's universal equality. At n=2, f=2>log22=1, refuting option 4. The strict lower bound cannot be replaced by equality at an integer: n<2k+1 is strict throughout the corresponding floor interval.

The ratio has no limit. At n=2k it equals one; at n=2k+1-1 it equals 2k/(2k+1-1)→1/2. A bounded oscillating ratio preserves tightness while defeating asymptotic equivalence to n. Compare 2⌈log2n⌉, whose analogous bounds are n≤f(n)<2n; that expression would match option 2.

Question 12. A factorial comparison using logarithms

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q71; MS_CS_1405_Q120. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Which statement is correct as n grows?

1.
n!∈O(2n)
2.
2n∈o(n!)
3.
n!∈Θ(nn)
4.
log(n!)∈Θ(n)
Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 2. At least the last ⌈n/2⌉ factorial factors are at least n/2. For n≥2,

n!≥(n/2)n/2,n!2n≥(n8)n/2→∞.

For example, once n≥16, the displayed lower bound is at least 2n/2 and hence unbounded. Its reciprocal tends to zero, proving 2n∈o(n!) and disproving option 1's proposed factorial upper bound.

Option 3 is also false. In n!/nn=∏j=1n(j/n), the first ⌊n/2⌋ factors are at most one half and the others at most one. Therefore the ratio is at most 2-⌊n/2⌋→0. This disproves the required positive lower constant for Θ(nn).

Finally, taking natural logarithms of elementary factorial bounds gives ln(n!)≤nlnn. For n≥4, the lower bound is at least (n/4)lnn, because ln(n/2)≥(lnn)/2. Thus ln(n!)∈Θ(nlnn), not Θ(n), eliminating option 4. No appeal to a memorized Stirling approximation is needed for these order statements.

These proofs assume the compared exponential base is fixed. They extend to any constant base B>1 by replacing nln2 with nlnB. They do not imply a factorial is tightly equivalent to a chosen exponential whose exponent merely has order nlnn; tight equivalence still requires controlling the actual ratio.

Integrated multistep challenges

Question 45. Oscillation across growth classes

Original integrated asymptotic challenge; not an authentic examination item.

For positive integer n, let f(n)=n2+sin(lnn) and g(n)=n2. Which relation holds? Construct integer subsequences and control their rounding errors in your proof.

1. f∈Θ(g)

2. f∈O(g) but not Ω(g)

3. f∈Ω(g) but not O(g)

4. Neither big-oh nor big-omega relation holds.

Read the full derivation, witnesses and counterexamples

Correct option: 4. Since g(n)=n2>0, the relevant ratio is R(n)=nsin(lnn). Merely saying the sine oscillates would not prove the existence of suitable integer subsequences, so construct them explicitly.

Let tk=π/2+2πk, xk=etk and nk=⌊xk⌋. The relative rounding error tends to zero, giving lnnk-tk→0. Continuity of sine then gives sin(lnnk)→1. Beyond a fixed index it is at least one half, so R(nk)≥nk→∞. Any proposed eventual upper constant is exceeded along this integer subsequence.

Similarly, let uk=3π/2+2πk and mk=⌊euk⌋. Then lnmk-uk→0 and sin(lnmk)→-1. Eventually it is at most negative one half, giving 0<R(mk)≤1/mk→0. Any proposed positive eventual lower constant fails on this second integer subsequence.

To justify the logarithmic rounding claim quantitatively, for x>1, 1-1/x≤⌊x⌋/x≤1. Its logarithm is trapped between ln(1-1/x) and zero, both tending to zero. Thus discretization does not remove either construction.

The first subsequence refutes O(g) and the second refutes Ω(g). Consequently options 1, 2 and 3 each assert a bound that fails. Although n≤f(n)≤n3 globally, those wider envelopes do not make f tightly quadratic. Also neither f∈o(g) nor f∈ω(g) holds: each would require one uniform ratio limit rather than these incompatible subsequences.

The complete derivation and assumptions are written above.

Input position in a binary block Example Normalized ratio
First integer n=8 8/8=1
Interior integer n=12 8/12=2/3

The floor's effect is bounded in the exponent by less than one, so it changes the power of two by a bounded factor. It can preserve a tight class while destroying exact equality and asymptotic equivalence. That precise distinction is more informative than saying floors can always be ignored.

Complete asymptotic rules and examination traps

1. Identify the function and its model

State whether the object is an exact operation count, a worst-case maximum, a distributional average or a randomized expectation. A statement about one input is not a worst-case bound. A bound on one algorithm is not automatically a lower bound for the whole problem.

2. Translate each bound into its quantifiers

For O, one upper constant and one threshold must work for every later input. For Ω, a positive lower constant must work on that same kind of tail. For Θ, both inequalities must hold. Constants may not change with the input being bounded.

3. Finite exceptions do not refute tail claims

A lower bound may start after a small zero or negative value if the function is eventually nonnegative. One small violation does not refute an asymptotic relation. To disprove it, construct violations beyond any proposed threshold.

4. Infinitely many successes are insufficient

An alternating function can satisfy a lower inequality on every odd input and fail it on every even input. An eventual bound requires all sufficiently large inputs. Check every unbounded parity class or other relevant subsequence.

5. Use the proper normalized ratio

Divide by the entire proposed comparison function, retaining coefficients and parentheses. If that denominator is eventually positive, ratio zero gives little-oh, a finite positive limit gives tightness and infinity gives little-omega. An undefined denominator requires another formulation.

6. A nonexistent limit is not a verdict

Inspect eventual upper and lower envelopes. Ratios alternating between one and three establish tightness; ratios approaching zero and infinity on separate subsequences refute both one-sided bounds. Oscillation by itself proves neither conclusion.

7. Tightness and equivalence are distinct

The relation f∼g requires ratio one. The relation f∈Θ(g) requires only positive finite envelopes. A ratio tending to seven proves the latter but not the former; a bounded oscillating ratio may prove tightness without any limit.

8. Strict bounds quantify over every constant

Little-oh requires the ratio to fall below every prescribed positive constant eventually. Little-omega requires it to exceed every such constant. Failure of a tight relation does not imply either strict relation when subsequences behave differently.

9. Upper bounds need not be tight

A function of tight order nlogn also belongs to O(n2). In a multiple-choice question using only O, more than one option can be literally true. Distinguish the mathematically true statements from a source's conventional request for the smallest listed upper bound.

10. Simplify cancellations before reading degrees

Compute the full expression before selecting its highest surviving power. Subtracting two quadratic expressions can leave zero, a linear function or another quadratic function. Subtracting unspecified Θ classes does not determine a tight answer.

11. Prove positivity for signed expressions

The default runtime convention is eventually nonnegative. If g>0 and |h|=o(g), an eventual bound |h|≤g/2 gives g/2≤g+h≤3g/2. This justifies lower-order signed perturbations without permitting arbitrary negative runtimes.

12. Use a conjugate for close square roots

The identity A-B=(A-B)/(A+B) exposes cancellations. For example, n2+n-n tends to one half, whereas n2+1-n has reciprocal-linear order. The leftover numerator determines the distinction.

13. Fixed logarithm bases change a constant

For fixed a,b>1, logan=(logbn)/(logba). This preserves tight order while changing exact values. If the base varies, redo the algebra: lognn=1 is not tightly logarithmic.

14. Iteration is different from a power

Write parentheses explicitly. The expressions log(logn), (logn)2 and log(n2) apply different operations. A nested exponential can collapse under iterated logarithms without making its full output small.

15. Recheck variable exponents

The polynomial-degree rule assumes a fixed exponent. Here n1/log2n=2 exactly, while nlog2n is larger than every fixed polynomial and smaller than 2n. Taking logarithms of ratios reveals which situation applies.

16. Distinguish coefficients inside and outside powers

A fixed positive factor outside an preserves its tight class. Replacing an by acn generally does not when a>1 and fixed c≠1. An additive unbounded change in the exponent can also destroy tightness.

17. Compare exponent differences directly

For fixed a>1, the quotient au/av=au-v. A bounded exponent difference yields tightness, and a difference tending to positive or negative infinity gives strict growth in the corresponding direction. Equal broad orders of u and v are insufficient.

18. Taking logarithms loses multiplicative precision

The logarithms of 2n2 and 2n2+n are equivalent, but the original ratio is 2n. A polynomial logarithm describes the quantity's scale of representation, not polynomial enumeration work. Do not exponentiate a broad tight class as though it were an exact identity.

19. Use the hierarchy with fixed hypotheses

For fixed positive k,ε and fixed a>1, (lnn)k=o(nε) and nε=o(an). If a power, base or coefficient varies with input, those fixed-parameter theorems may not apply.

20. Factorial bounds can be elementary

The sandwich (n/2)n/2≤n!≤nn for n≥2 yields ln(n!)∈Θ(nlnn). A fixed-base exponential is strict smaller order than n!, while n!=o(nn). A sharper approximation is unnecessary for these class statements.

21. Round integer capacities upward

The least nonnegative h with 2h≥M is ⌈log2M⌉ for integer M≥1. Check neighboring powers rather than rely on floating-point rounding. Having enough leaves is a necessary capacity condition, not proof of an attainable optimal algorithm.

22. Floors inside exponentials need control

The exact bound n/2<2⌊log2n⌋≤n preserves tight linear order. Its ratio alternates through binary blocks and has no unique limit. A bounded rounding change can preserve tightness while destroying equivalence.

23. A factorial argument shift can matter

The ratio (2n)!/n!=∏j=n+12nj is unbounded. The corresponding logarithms still share tight nlogn order. Tight equivalence of logarithms cannot be transferred back to the factorials.

24. Fixed-index binomial coefficients are a special case

For fixed r, (nr)/nr→1/r!. If r varies with n, neither the factorial denominator nor the number of factors is fixed. The fixed-degree polynomial proof cannot be reused without its hypothesis.

25. Harmonic growth is not exact logarithmic equality

The bounds ln(n+1)≤Hn≤1+lnn prove logarithmic order and equivalence to lnn. Exact partial sums remain rational sums of unequal reciprocals. Divergence says the sum is unbounded; it does not imply linear growth.

26. The maximum rule needs a uniform multiplier

For a fixed number r of nonnegative summands, the sum lies between the maximum and r times that maximum. A growing term count can introduce another factor, and opposite signs can cancel. In special varying-count families, prove a bounded multiplier explicitly.

27. Products and transitivity combine witnesses

Multiply nonnegative upper inequalities to obtain a product upper bound, and combine both sides for a tight product. Take the maximum of the original thresholds. Transitivity multiplies witness constants, which remain independent of input.

28. Reciprocation reverses inequalities

If 0<f≤cg eventually, then 1/f≥1/(cg). Thus an upper bound becomes a reciprocal lower bound, rather than automatically a reciprocal tight bound. Two-sided positive witnesses are required to preserve tightness under inversion.

29. Composition must reach the original tail

Substituting an inner argument tending to infinity preserves a valid eventual inequality if it stays in the domain. A bounded inner argument may keep hitting values outside the proven tail. Applying an outer exponential to the values is a different operation and may amplify constants into unbounded ratios.

30. Declare the multivariate domain and tail

A joint-tail convention requires both parameters past their own thresholds. A combined-size convention can include one parameter fixed. Test allowed paths that grow both variables when needed, and retain graph or matrix restrictions before simplifying.

31. Count significant recurrence levels and their tolls

A shrinking one-branch recurrence with squared-logarithm toll can accumulate cubic-logarithm cost. A square-root recurrence should be studied in logarithmic size, with floors and a terminating base region controlled. Multiplying recurrences require products or logarithms, not additive toll formulas.

32. Finite graphs illustrate; proofs establish tails

A plotted prefix cannot certify a uniform bound over infinitely many inputs. Use explicit witnesses, justified limits or counterexample subsequences to prove the claim. Finite crossovers remain separate exact calculations even after the tight classes are known.
